options: A cloud provider's SLA for data durability
The tendency for applications and compute to be pulled toward the location of a large, existing dataset, because moving the data is far more expensive and slower than moving the compute
A compression algorithm used in cross-cloud transfers
The physical weight limit on a storage appliance
questions.explain: Data gravity, a term coined by Dave McCrory in 2010, describes how large datasets attract workloads toward them because moving large amounts of data is slow and expensive compared to moving compute.

questions.q: Why is it usually cheaper to move compute to data rather than data to compute, at large scale?
options: Cloud providers never charge for moving compute between regions
Data cannot legally be moved between clouds under any circumstance
Moving data is always technically impossible once it exceeds 1 TB
Compute is comparatively cheap and fast to redeploy, while moving terabytes or petabytes incurs real egress cost, real transfer time, and operational inertia
questions.explain: A compute job can be redeployed elsewhere in minutes, while moving large datasets costs real money in egress fees, takes real time, and disrupts the operational surface (pipelines, access controls, backups) built around the data's current location.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is egress cost?
options: The per-gigabyte fee a cloud provider charges to move data out of its network toward another cloud or the public internet
A one-time fee charged only when an account is first created
A discount applied for high-volume customers
The cost of running a Kubernetes cluster
questions.explain: Egress cost is the per-gigabyte fee for moving data out of a cloud's network, and it applies to cross-cloud transfers the same way it applies to transfers to the public internet.

questions.q: A company standardizes compute on Azure, but a 40 TB dataset has lived in AWS S3 for years. According to this lesson, what does data gravity predict will happen to a new analytics workload needing that dataset?
options: The dataset will be freely and instantly mirrored to Azure with no cost or time impact
The workload will likely still end up running in AWS, next to the data, despite the stated Azure standardization preference
The company's cloud strategy document automatically overrides data gravity
Data gravity only applies to datasets smaller than 1 GB
questions.explain: Data gravity frequently overrides stated architectural preferences — the economical choice is to run the new workload next to the large existing dataset rather than pay to move the dataset to match a standardization goal.

questions.q: What practical implication does this lesson draw about where a new large data source should first be stored?
options: It doesn't matter, since data can always be moved later for free
It should be chosen randomly by whichever team provisions storage first
The initial storage location should be treated as a long-lived architectural commitment, because gravity compounds and reversing it later gets more expensive over time
It should always default to on-premises storage regardless of workload needs
questions.explain: Because data gravity compounds as downstream consumers accumulate, the decision about where a large dataset first lands is disproportionately expensive to reverse later, so it deserves deliberate, early architectural attention.
